Executive function across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Executive functions undergo rapid improvement during the preschool years. Many executive abilities that are fragile or inconsistent in 3-year-olds become reliably measurable by age 4, and they strengthen further by age 5. This means that between 4 and 5, children become noticeably better at focusing attention, following multi-step rules, controlling impulses, and switching flexibly between different tasks or mental sets. Five-year-olds can play games that involve withholding an action (like "Red Light, Green Light" or "Freeze dance") and typically follow rules like "wait your turn" in group settings with only occasional reminders. Experimental tasks such as the Day-Night Stroop (where children must say "night" when shown a sun card, and "day" for a moon card) illustrate the improvement: 4-year-olds often struggle to maintain accuracy throughout the task, whereas 5-year-olds show markedly better interference control and can sustain the rule for more trials 1, reflecting maturation of frontal-striatal circuits supporting response inhibition. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Working memory also expands between 4 and 5. A 3-year-old can typically keep  2 items in mind (e.g. simple instructions like "touch your nose and clap your hands"), and a 4-year-old about 3 items. By age 5, children can often manage 4-step instructions or remember a sequence of 4 digits or words, especially if they practice some informal strategies like self-repetition 2. In practical terms, a five-year-old can more reliably follow complex directions such as, "Go to your room, get your shoes, then come to the kitchen and put them on," while a 4-year-old might get sidetracked or forget one of the steps. Five-year-olds increasingly recruit verbal self-instructions to keep rules active ("say the rule to do the rule"), which is a known strategy to boost working memory and cognitive control (and helps explain why linguistic advances at this age amplify executive performance) 3. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Cognitive flexibility also undergoes a step change; here, we continue referring to the classic Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS) task. Three-year-olds will perseverate on the first rule given (e.g., sorting cards by color) and struggle to switch to a new rule (sorting by shape) even when they know the rule changed; they’ll verbally acknowledge the new rule but still sort cards wrongly according to the old rule 4. By 4 years old, children can successfully switch to the new sorting rule after a few reminder trials 4 (considered a fundamental cognitive milestone). By age 5, cognitive flexibility is more robust: five-year-olds not only switch rules, but can sometimes handle a more complex sequence of switches or hierarchical rules (for instance, sorting by shape only if a border on the card is a certain color) 5, 4. They still cannot match the flexibility of older children (for example, 5-year-olds will struggle with switching rules on every trial, a level of flexibility seen around 7-8 years 5), but they are clearly more adaptable than preschoolers just a year younger. In everyday life, this translates to coping better with changing plans or contexts: a 5-year-old is more likely than a 4-year-old to handle a sudden schedule change with only minor upset or to understand that "at school we do it this way, even if at home we do it that way".

This age is sometimes termed an "executive function sweet spot" in that children make noticeable gains that parents and teachers can see: they become better at cleaning up with a routine, following classroom rules, and verbalizing strategies (like saying "I have to wait, so I’m counting to 10") 6. Not coincidentally, many interventions to promote school readiness target executive skills at this age, using games and play to strengthen self-control and flexibility 7. Overall, five-year-olds can hold more information in mind, resist more impulses, and shift rules more readily than they could a year prior, forming the cognitive foundation for the structured learning environment of kindergarten.
